intro:
AI phone ordering works by answering your restaurant’s calls, taking the order, and sending it to the kitchen. For a busy shop, it can handle pickup and delivery orders, simple menu questions, and basic requests without making your staff stop what they are doing.

The useful questions are the practical ones: what it can take, what it cannot take, how the phone forwarding works, and what it costs on a real month. Below, I’ll answer those owner questions in plain English and show where ROAL fits in.

sections.h2: What does AI phone ordering actually do on a real call?
sections.body:
A good restaurant phone host should do the basics well, not sound fancy. ROAL answers the phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, confirms the order back, quotes a ready time, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

It also handles the common stuff that eats up your counter time:
- Hours
- Address
- Parking
- Menu questions
- Reservation requests
- Language switching when the caller speaks another language
- Caller name and phone number

It should also know when to stop. If the caller asks about catering, a complaint, an allergy-sensitive order, or wants a manager, the host sends that to staff with a summary. It does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes payment.

A simple phone script line sounds like this: “Thanks for calling Tony’s Pizza. Would you like pickup or delivery today?” That kind of opening gets to the order fast and keeps the call moving.

sections.h2: What should I ask before I try AI phone ordering?
sections.body:
Owners usually want to know the same few things before they try a phone host. Keep your questions tight and practical.

Use this checklist:
1. Can it read my menu and prices from my website or menu PDF?
2. Can it take sizes, modifiers, and notes the way my staff does?
3. What happens when it does not know an answer?
4. Can it hand off allergy calls and manager requests?
5. Does it take card numbers, or does payment stay the way we already do it?
6. Can I hear the call transcript and listen back later?

ROAL is set up for this kind of workflow. You paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try, and it reads public pages and menu files to build a phone host in about two minutes. You can test-call it right in the browser with no sign-up needed.

A useful test line is: “I want a large pepperoni, light sauce, no onions, and extra cheese.” If your menu has modifiers and notes, you want to see whether the host captures them cleanly before you go live.

sections.h2: How do I forward my restaurant number without losing it?
sections.body:
You keep your restaurant’s own number. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your existing number to it. You can forward all calls, or only when the line is busy or unanswered. Forwarding can be turned off any time.

The exact steps depend on your carrier or phone system, so always confirm with them and test with a real call. Common patterns include:
- Many landlines and some carriers: dial *72 and then the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off
- Some GSM mobile carriers: **21*number# forwards all calls, ##21# turns it off, **61*number# forwards unanswered calls, and **67*number# forwards busy calls
- Verizon Wireless: *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding
- Business VoIP systems: usually set forwarding in the web portal

A practical owner setup looks like this: keep your number on the menu, forward it during lunch and dinner rush, then turn it off if you want the staff to pick up again. If you want a carrier-by-carrier cheat sheet, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

A good test script is: “Call my store number, let it ring twice, and make sure the forwarded call reaches the host.”

sections.h2: What happens when the host does not know the answer?
sections.body:
No phone host knows everything, especially for a real restaurant with changing specials and edge cases. When ROAL cannot answer a question, it sends it to your inbox. You answer it once, and the host knows it from then on.

That setup is useful for the questions that come up all the time but are not always on the menu page:
- “Do you have a gluten-free crust today?”
- “Can you swap the side on this combo?”
- “Do you park behind the building?”
- “Can you hold the order for 20 minutes?”

For harder calls, it should hand off cleanly to staff. That includes catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests. The goal is not to trap the caller in a loop. It is to get the easy orders off your plate and move the tricky ones to a person.

A useful staff note format is:
- Caller name
- Phone number
- Order request
- What was asked
- What needs follow-up

That way, the person taking over has context instead of starting cold. If you want a deeper look at call transfer behavior, see [transferring calls from AI to a person](/blog/ai-phone-host-transfer-to-staff) and [when the AI doesn’t know the answer](/blog/ai-phone-host-unanswered-questions).

sections.h2: Is AI phone ordering a good fit for my kind of restaurant?
sections.body:
It tends to make the most sense for places with repeated phone work: pizza shops, takeout spots, delis, family restaurants, diners, and multi-location groups. If your phone rings a lot for pickup orders, hours, menu questions, or delivery details, a phone host can take real pressure off the front counter.

Here is a quick fit check:
- Good fit: you take many pickup orders by phone
- Good fit: customers ask the same questions all day
- Good fit: you have a live menu that changes sometimes
- Less fit: most orders are already handled another way
- Less fit: you need card payment taken over the phone

ROAL was built by Venkata Vamsi, a founder in Jersey City, NJ, and the first restaurants using it are in Jersey City and Hoboken, though it works for any US restaurant. It also has a dashboard for live tickets, call history, menu editing, and multi-location menus, which helps if you run more than one store.

If you want a simple owner-minded framing, ask this: “How many calls does my team answer that could be handled by a clean phone script and a good menu?” If the answer is a lot, AI phone ordering is worth testing. If you want the broader context, [ROAL facts](/facts) and [how it works](/how-it-works) are the two pages to read next.
